issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the other two memory items, which describe intrusive, sensory-dominated, repeatedly replaying trauma memories. That combination is not impossible, but with no other items indicating organized narrative access, the 'very easily' wording pulls in the opposite direction and is clinically inconsistent within this node.

issues.item: Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of mugging/robbery. 'Being around children' and 'Happy families' do not show a plausible thematic link to the reported trauma, and there are no accompanying threat or appraisal items to explain why these social/family cues would specifically trigger this patient's robbery-related PTSD.

issues.item: Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
issues.explanation: 'I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma' is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The formulation mainly links triggers and memory with maladaptive strategies, but the actual triggers and memory content given are socially/family themed and intrusive-image based; deliberate conflict-seeking does not fit clearly with those items and looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, triggers centered on children and idealized families are hard to link clinically unless there is additional trauma meaning not represented elsewhere. The memory items describe perceptual re-experiencing of the robbery, but these triggers imply family/child themes that are absent from the rest of the profile, making the trigger set feel disconnected from the trauma type.

Within the Triggers node, 'children present' and 'happy families' suggest a loss/family-comparison theme, whereas 'being criticised or corrected' suggests interpersonal shame or sensitivity. These could coexist, but together they do not form a coherent trigger pattern tied to a robbery, especially given no threat or appraisal items supporting these meanings.

'Happy families' is a weakly plausible trigger for a mugging/robbery trauma and is hard to connect to the accompanying memory items, which are purely sensory/reliving-based and suggest trauma reminders tied more directly to the event. It does not fit well with the otherwise robbery-linked trigger pattern.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking conflict/create drama' is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The formulation links triggers and memory to maladaptive strategies, but the selected triggers and memory items imply intrusive re-experiencing, for which suppression/avoidance is coherent; deliberate conflict-seeking appears clinically disconnected and unusually externalising relative to the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Kwame was 58 years old, married, and had spent most of his working life as a hairdresser, a trade that kept him in close contact with people all day and required him to stay calm, attentive, and precise. Before the trauma, he had built his routine around the steady rhythm of the salon: conversations with regular clients, the familiar smell of products and shampoo, the small corrections that came with the work. The robbery happened late one evening as he was leaving a shop after closing up for the day. He noticed two men nearby acting in a way that unsettled him; they seemed suspicious, lingering without purpose and watching him too closely. Before he could make sense of what was happening, they mugged him, and the suddenness of it left him feeling exposed and overpowered. He later described the event as something he understood happened, yet when he tried to talk about it, the words would not come. What remained were pictures: the look of the men, the instant of threat, flashes of movement and fear. He said it was like a film that played over and over, with the same frightening images returning even when he wanted nothing more than to push them away.

In the weeks that followed, Kwame found that certain moments in ordinary life could bring the robbery sharply back to him. If a customer or family member corrected him or spoke critically, he would feel a sudden tightening inside, as though he were being put on the spot again and needed to defend himself. He became especially uneasy around people who seemed suspicious to him, such as strangers lingering outside the salon window or anyone he read as watching too long or moving unpredictably. At work, where he had once felt confident moving between chairs and clients, he began to watch people more carefully, scanning faces and posture while trying to keep his attention on the haircut in front of him. The smell of alcohol was another immediate reminder; if someone came in smelling of liquor, or if he caught that odor nearby, he would feel abruptly on edge, as though the atmosphere around him had changed and danger might follow. These reactions were not limited to rare moments. They began to shape how he moved through the day, quietly narrowing the spaces he felt able to occupy.

Kwame also found himself turning the event over in his mind, dwelling on what he believed he had done wrong. He replayed the path he had taken that evening, the time he left, the decisions he made, and whether he should have noticed the men sooner or avoided the area altogether. He was burdened by the sense that he had failed to protect himself in some way, and he kept returning to those thoughts in an effort to make the event feel more understandable. At the same time, he tried hard not to think about the robbery at all. He would push the memories away when they surfaced and refuse to let himself dwell on them, but the effort left him tense and preoccupied. The more he tried to avoid the experience in his mind, the more aware he seemed of how often it sat just beneath the surface. He also began avoiding other people more broadly. Outside of work, he cut down on social contact, kept to himself when he could, and found excuses not to spend time in crowded or unfamiliar places. Even in the salon, where he still worked, he kept more distance than before and felt less inclined to engage in the easy conversation that once came naturally.

By the time he sought help, these changes had become hard to ignore. His wife had noticed that he was quieter and more withdrawn, and his work life had become more constrained by his vigilance and discomfort. Kwame came to treatment saying that he wanted to “get back to normal,” but he spoke with the same struggle for words that marked his memory of the mugging itself. He could describe the robbery only in fragments, almost as if he were showing pieces of an image rather than telling a story. What finally brought him in was the growing sense that he could not keep living this way, always bracing for criticism, suspicious of people’s intentions, and on guard whenever he caught the smell of alcohol. He was most afraid that the robbery had changed him in a way he could not simply will away, yet he still hoped that talking about it might make the pictures less overwhelming and allow him to move through his days with less fear.
